In one sentence: biostatisticians are not just running a regression; they turn clinical, public health, or life science questions into a reviewable study design, analysis plan, statistical inference, and statement of limitations. The U.S. counterpart is O*NET-SOC 15-2041.01, marked Bright Outlook and listed as Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed). The core boundary is that you can decide the statistical method, the analysis definition, and how far the results can be interpreted, but you cannot make medical judgments for the clinical team, and you cannot write statistical output directly as diagnosis, release, or regulatory conclusions.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to first write the question as testable endpoints and hypotheses and to compute the sample size before modeling; you can accept having your analysis plan, code, and results reviewed point by point by others; when data are missing, the protocol deviates, or results cannot be explained, you are willing to stop, record, and state the limitations rather than force out a good-looking conclusion; and your interest in how far a conclusion can be supported exceeds your interest in whether the model ran.

Conditions for pausing major investment: you have not yet completed, under supervision, one full closed loop from research question to analysis plan, data processing, result interpretation, and statement of limitations; or you only want to use the output of an off-the-shelf model to obtain a significant conclusion and are unwilling to bear responsibility for the analysis plan, data quality, and traceable records; also, do not treat being able to use one statistics software package or having taken a few statistics courses as proof that you can independently sign off on research conclusions.

Education, qualifications, and job authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Five (SVP 8.0 and above), and among respondents 58% consider a master's degree necessary, 29% a doctorate, and 13% a bachelor's degree; BLS lists a master's degree as the typical entry-level education for the statistician series. These are survey and public material definitions, not a uniform statutory threshold; real requirements are set by the employer, funder, ethics committee, and local regulations, and signing and data access permissions additionally require institutional authorization.

In one sentence: this is a professional role centered on study design, statistical analysis, data quality, and conclusion boundaries, and its output is reviewable analysis plans, results, and statements of limitations, not decisions made in place of physicians or regulators. The U.S. wage and employment data follow the Statisticians definition (SOC 15-2041) rather than a separate 15-2041.01 listing; mainland China has no national occupation-level wage statistics corresponding to this occupation, and this page marks this honestly rather than filling in figures.

The work of biostatisticians falls into three categories: first, study design and inference tasks (clarifying questions and endpoints with clinical or life science teams, computing sample sizes, choosing analysis methods, and interpreting how far the results can support conclusions); second, data and computing tasks (cleaning and checking data, writing analysis code, building or maintaining biological data databases, and monitoring trial data quality); third, communication and documentation tasks (writing analysis plans and results reports, submitting statistical materials to data monitoring committees or regulatory agencies, and taking part in protocol review and papers). All three share the same reviewable chain of evidence.
Clinical and epidemiological research tasks

Clarify the research question and endpoints → determine the design and comparisons with the clinical team → compute the sample size → write the analysis plan and predefine the analysis population and the method for handling missing data → analyze clinical or survey data → interpret effect sizes and uncertainty → record limitations and deviations → submit results for review and submission.
Data and computing tasks

Verify data sources and coding → check missing values and anomalies → write reproducible analysis code in SAS, R, or Python and similar tools → produce tables and figures → perform sensitivity analysis and model diagnostics → keep the code, data versions, and analysis logs so that others can rerun and obtain the same results.

Collaborate with researchers, clinicians, data managers, and ethics and regulatory personnel, write analysis plans and results reports, explain statistical issues to data monitoring committees or regulatory agencies, guide statistical assistants or programmers, and state clearly when the methods or data cannot support a conclusion rather than forcing one out.

Adjacent directions should be verified by their real subject matter and tasks: the statistician parent category may include biostatistics, agriculture, and economics; data scientists may also do research analysis rather than only prediction products; clinical research coordinators plan, manage, and coordinate trials and may also evaluate analysis data; bioinformatics research involves omics, algorithms, and statistics; and mathematicians include basic and applied mathematics research, not only pure theory. Transition gaps are an editorial analysis and do not automatically exchange responsibilities.
Core purpose
Use reviewable statistical methods so that questions in life science, clinical, and public health research receive conclusions with a basis and a statement of uncertainty.
Main subjects and basis

The subjects are clinical and survey data, trial protocols, and biological data; the basis is the study protocol, the statistical analysis plan, statistical methods, and the applicable ethics and regulatory requirements.
Core process
Design the study, compute the sample size, write the analysis plan, clean and check the data, model and infer, interpret results, and record limitations.
Main outputs
Reviewable statistical analysis plans, analysis dataset documentation, results tables and figures, methodological descriptions, study limitation statements, and statistical materials for submission.
Responsible party

Statistical methods and analysis conclusions are the responsibility of trained and authorized biostatistical personnel; medical judgments are the responsibility of clinical researchers and physicians; regulatory conclusions are made by regulatory agencies; when work exceeds your authorization you should escalate rather than decide on your own.
Permissions and approval

Whether you may access identifiable participant data, sign statistical reports, or submit materials externally is determined jointly by the institutional authorization chain, ethics approval, and regulations, and does not arise automatically from job grade or software skills.
Conclusion boundaries

Statistical results describe the inferences and uncertainty supportable under a given design and dataset; they are not the same as a clinical efficacy conclusion and do not replace medical, ethical, or regulatory judgment, and they are affected by sample size, missing data, multiple comparisons, and protocol deviations.

Before starting, verify at least six items: the occupation definition and the job entity, the education and training pathway, the actual scope of use of statistical methods and software, authorization to access data and participant information, the review mechanism for analysis plans and records, and the real pay structure and working hours.
Occupation definition

Insufficient evidence: this round did not find a formal detailed category code in the mainland China occupational classification that corresponds one-to-one with biostatisticians. The U.S. code is O*NET-SOC15-2041.01; Chinese positions must be verified by institution, tasks, and competent authority requirements, and the absence of the classification cannot be asserted merely from a same-named position.
Education and training pathway

O*NET lists it as Job Zone Five, and respondents consider a master's degree necessary at 58%, a doctorate at 29%, and a bachelor's degree at 13%; BLS lists a master's degree as the typical entry-level education for the statistician series. Coursework and training in statistics, biostatistics, applied mathematics, and epidemiology are common foundations.
Methods and tools

O*NET uses Lightcast data on unique job postings across the United States in 2025: among postings linked to 15-2041.01, SAS appears in 66%, R61%, Python17%, and SQL9%. This is a job advertisement skills signal, not an adoption rate for all employers or practitioners.
Data and privacy authorization

Clinical and genetic data may contain personal information and cannot be uniformly assumed to be identifiable. Personal information processing requires verifying identifiability, purpose, permissions, and the lawful bases under Article 13; medical and health data are sensitive personal information, and consent-based processing requires verifying separate consent and related conditions; anonymized information is not the same as de-identified information that can still be re-identified. Human genetic resources should be verified by the material and information definitions and specific activities of the 2024 regulations, with the health department as the competent authority, and not all statistical, animal, or anonymized data are treated as the same type of human genetic resources permission.
Records and review

Editorial suggestion: make the analysis plan, code, data, and logs mutually traceable, verify reviewers and signing arrangements with the institution, and record the reasons for and impact of changes to analysis definitions; do not assume that all institutions use the same second-person review approach.
Pay and working hours

The same job title may be paid by annual salary, by project, or under institutional establishment; when comparing, include data access permissions, review responsibility, overtime during submission crunch periods, continuing education costs, and whether there is mentoring by a statistical lead in the written agreement.

Biostatisticians (U.S. counterpart O*NET-SOC 15-2041.01, Biostatisticians) apply biostatistical theory and methods to life science research: working with physicians, life scientists, or other professionals to design studies, computing sample sizes for clinical research, writing analysis plans and analysis results statements, writing code with statistical software to analyze clinical or survey data, and explaining results and limitations to research teams, data monitoring committees, or regulatory agencies. It is neither a data entry position nor one that carries diagnostic or prescribing responsibility.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 15-2041.01 Biostatisticians, Bright Outlook, updated 2026. The official duty is to develop and apply biostatistical theory and methods for life science research; the main work activities are analyzing data or information (importance 92), using computers (91), communicating with supervisors and colleagues (84), making decisions and solving problems (81), and interpreting the meaning of information for others (79).

U.S. wage distribution: the 2025 BLS occupational employment and wage statistics (OEWS) shown by O*NET, under the Statisticians definition (SOC 15-2041) — annual wage 64,000 USD at the 10th percentile, 82,220 USD at the 25th percentile, 105,650 USD at the median, 141,490 USD at the 75th percentile, and 174,050 USD at the 90th percentile; the corresponding median hourly wage is 50.79 USD. This definition is not a separate 15-2041.01 statistic.

Precise Chinese occupation wages are still missing; the authorized salary module lists matched NBS2025 industry and broad personnel category annual average references, which cannot replace occupation wages.

BLS 2025—2035 projections for Statisticians (SOC 15-2041, statistician parent category proxy definition): about 31,300 in 2025 and about 34,700 in 2035, growth of 11.0%, net growth of about 3,400, and about 1,900 job openings per year; this is not a separate biostatistician 15-2041.01 statistic.

2025 U.S. Statisticians SOC15-2041 parent category industry distribution: professional, scientific, and technical services 30%, government 26%, education 15%, and other 29% (including health care and social assistance and finance and insurance); other is an item actually published by the source, not a residual calculated on this page. It cannot be treated as a separate biostatistician 15-2041.01 figure, a Chinese employer distribution, or industry wages. Unique U.S. job postings in 2025 list 29 software skills: SAS66%, R61%, Python17%, SAP11%, and SQL9%; these are not on-the-job adoption rates.

paragraphs: This page compares biostatisticians with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and output, key differences, and which direction better fits each preference. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean job titles are interchangeable.

Evidence note: this occupation and statisticians are based on O*NET15-2041.01 and 15-2041.00; the other directions were verified against the 15-2051.00, 11-9121.01, 19-1029.01, and 15-2021.00 task pages respectively, all U.S. definitions. The table below is an editorial summary of common task emphasis, and overlapping tasks cannot be separated absolutely; education, qualifications, and authorization must be verified separately by jurisdiction and institution.

The table below compares biostatisticians with adjacent occupations and the pathways for moving in from adjacent positions; the basis for judgment is the main output, the object of responsibility, and the required training, not how similar the job titles are.
Statisticians (SOC 15-2041.00)
Directed at broader statistical inference and method problems, with outputs mainly being statistical models, method descriptions, and data analysis reports.

The two share similar methodological foundations, but biostatisticians by default face life science, clinical, and public health questions and must handle trial design, participant data, and the ethics and regulatory context; statisticians do not take this as the default scenario.

If you want the method itself and cross-industry application as your main line, consider statistics first; if your interest is concentrated in clinical and life science questions, consider biostatistics first.
Data Scientists (15-2051.00)
Work centers on general data products or prediction models, with outputs mainly being features, models, evaluation metrics, and data products.

Data scientists focus more on predictive performance and productization, and the evaluation standard is often model metrics; biostatisticians focus on effect estimation, uncertainty, and predefined inference questions, and the evaluation standard is whether the conclusion can support a research judgment.

If you would rather do end-to-end data products and prediction optimization, compare data science first; if you care more about the rigor of causal and effect estimation, consider biostatistics first.
Clinical Research Coordinators (11-9121.01)
Responsible for trial site execution: participant screening and follow-up, informed consent, and records and monitoring support.

Clinical research coordinators center on site execution and participant management, while biostatisticians center on design and inference; the two work closely together on protocols and data, but the object of responsibility and the required training differ.

If you would rather deal directly with people and organize site processes, compare clinical research coordination first; if you would rather handle design and inference problems, consider biostatistics first.
Bioinformatics Scientists (19-1029.01)
Develop algorithms and pipelines around omics and biological big data, with outputs mainly being computational pipelines, annotations, and bioinformatics analyses.

Bioinformatics scientists lean more toward algorithms, data structures, and mining biological mechanisms; biostatisticians lean more toward study design and statistical inference; both may handle large amounts of data, but the problem types and evaluation standards differ.
If you would rather write algorithms and handle omics data, consider bioinformatics first; if you would rather answer whether a study can support a conclusion, consider biostatistics first.
Mathematicians (15-2021.00)
Output is mathematical theory, proofs, and modeling methods themselves, and the application domain is not limited to the life sciences.

Mathematicians produce theoretical contributions and formal proofs as their main result, while biostatisticians produce explainable statistical conclusions within specific studies as their main result.
If you enjoy theoretical derivation and proof more, compare mathematics first; if you would rather apply methods to real research questions, consider biostatistics first.
Moving in from biomedical experimental or clinical positions
You already have experimental, clinical, or data management experience and want to move toward study design and statistical inference.

The gap is usually not biological or clinical knowledge but probability and statistical inference, study design, reproducible computing, and data responsibility; having done experiments or managed data is not the same as being able to independently bear statistical analysis responsibility.

If you are willing to build up statistical inference and programming training and accept review, you can consider moving in; if you only want to change the job title without building the methodological foundation, the gap will be large.

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main output, the object of responsibility, and the required methodological training, not how similar the names are; once the direction is set, verify item by item the target direction's education requirements, the actual scope of use of statistical methods and software, data access authorization, and the review mechanism, and keep written confirmation.

values: Education and training

U.S. side: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Five (SVP 8.0 and above), and among respondents 58% consider a master's degree necessary, 29% a doctorate, and 13% a bachelor's degree. BLS lists a master's degree as the typical entry-level education for the combined mathematicians and statisticians series, but notes that some positions accept a bachelor's degree.
The two definitions differ (O*NET is a respondent estimate, BLS is a series definition) and must be labeled separately; they cannot be combined into one threshold.
Data and compliance

When participant data are involved, first verify the applicable ethics rules, data use agreement, and institutional access rules; anonymized and identifiable information are judged separately. When China's human genetic resources are involved, verify ethics, informed consent, and the corresponding approval or filing conditions by activity under the 2024 revised regulations; international cooperative clinical trials have limited filing exceptions, and security review has applicable trigger conditions, so not all activities simultaneously require approval, filing, and security review.

Processing personal information (including sensitive personal information such as medical and health data) must comply with the Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China regarding notice, consent, least necessity, and impact assessment.
Tasks and work styles

The official skills profile centers on mathematics (91), critical thinking, reading comprehension, science, speaking, writing, and active learning; among transferable skills, complex problem solving and judgment and decision making both have importance 75. The main work activities are analyzing data or information (92), using computers (91), and interpreting the meaning of information for others (79).
The interest code is IC (Investigative and Conventional); these fields describe the characteristics of the occupational group and do not constitute an individual competence threshold.
Job posting technology signals

The O*NET technology list shows 29 software skills, mainly SAS 66%, R 61%, Python 17%, SAP 11%, and SQL 9%. These tools are used for data management, statistical modeling, reproducible analysis, and results presentation, and do not change method choice or conclusion responsibility.
Before using tools on clinical or genetic data, confirm whether ethics approval, the data use agreement, and access control cover that use.

items.title: What evidence employers usually look for

values: Fictional study package (not clinical evidence)

Generate 120 rows: 60 cases each for A and B, with j=1…60 within each group; id is the group name plus j, and age=20+(j mod 40). The primary endpoint is the 8-week continuous quantity Y (points, lower is better); when j≤50, A=100+((j−1) mod 10−4.5) and B=96+the same congruence term; when j>50, Y is left missing and missing=1, otherwise missing=0. The group labels are demonstration labels only and do not claim real randomization; no secondary endpoints are given, so no additional tests may be invented.

Write the plan in the first 60 minutes and generate and analyze the data by fixed rules in the next 45 minutes; use any statistical software and no real participant data. The 120 cases are the given scenario, not a validated sample size; the role is only that of a learner submitting a draft.
Tasks and deliverables

First specify the B−A mean difference, the complete-case analysis, the sample variance denominator n−1, and the approximate 95% interval formula d±1.96×sqrt(sA² ÷ nA + sB² ÷ nB). Report the original 120 cases, the 10 missing cases per group, and the observed sample of 50 per group; the missingness mechanism cannot be inferred backward from the data.

Sensitivity: compare only the mean difference over all 120 cases. Scenario S1 gives A missing values of 110 and B of 86; S2 gives A missing values of 90 and B of 106. Write the two differences and three limitations: this is a fictional non-randomized demonstration, the missingness mechanism is unknown, and the normal approximation interval is not a formal trial conclusion.
Reference calculation and interpretation

In the complete case the two group means are 100 and 96, each with n=50 and sample variance 8.418367; B−A=−4.000, SE=0.580288, and the given normal approximation 95% interval is [−5.137365, −2.862635]. It describes only the self-generated observed sample and cannot prove treatment efficacy or a real causal effect.

S1 mean difference over all 120 cases −7.333333; S2 −0.666667. The direction does not change under the given scenarios but the magnitude changes markedly; this does not prove the real missingness mechanism or a robust clinical benefit, and imputed values are not treated as additional independent observations to compute narrower intervals. Save the code, data rules, plan, and deviation records.
Boundary and scoring

Editorial scoring out of 10: input and missing data checks 2 points, mean variance and interval 3 points, the two sensitivity analyses 2 points, and limitations and record keeping 3 points; this is not a qualification or competence threshold. Stop immediately and switch to self-generated materials if real identifiable information is found; when external review is unavailable, note that no professional review was obtained.
Plan and data description

Submit the above 120-case rules, variable dictionary, and predefined analysis plan; note that the missingness mechanism is unknown and state the mean difference direction and the given interval algorithm.
Review and revision records

Keep the checks for each group of 50 complete cases, the sample variance, and the two imputation scenarios; attach comments if professional review can be obtained, otherwise honestly state the scope of self-review.
One-page results statement
Attach −4.000 and the approximation interval, S1 −7.333333, and S2 −0.666667, and write the limitations item by item; do not write it as real patient benefit or proof of practice.
Rerunnable script
The script generates the 120 rows from fixed formulas, with software version and run records attached; when generative tools are used, note the assisted scope and manual corrections.

values: Day one: task boundaries
Read the O*NET tasks and distinguish statistical design, programming, and clinical decisions; deliver a one-page boundary comparison.
Day two: data and permissions
Generate the 120 rows and dictionary as given, and check the 60 cases and 10 missing cases per group; use only fictional data and list the authorizations that would need checking on a real project.
Day three: write the plan first
Fix B−A, the complete-case analysis, the interval formula, and S1/S2; deliver the predefined plan and do not treat 120 as a validated sample size.
Day four: check the input
Check group by group that 50 cases are usable, the missing markers, the age range, and the coding; save the data version and processing log.
Day five: analysis and limitations
Rerun −4 and the given interval and the two sensitivity differences; write three limitations and deliver the draft results.
Day six: review feedback
Ask an experienced person to check the code and interpretation; if external feedback is unavailable, state that, complete only self-checks, and list the open questions.
Day seven: decide the next step

Organize the plan, script, results, and review boundaries, and decide from actual behavior whether to continue, pause, or compare adjacent directions; one exercise does not prove occupational competence.

entries: Continue: you can complete all outputs within seven days and are willing to accept item-by-item review of the analysis plan and code.

Change direction: you enjoy writing code or organizing data more than bearing responsibility for conclusions; compare data engineering or data management directions.

Fill in the evidence: organize the seven-day outputs into reviewable analysis work for course applications or job interviews.

entries.answer: Biostatisticians turn life science, clinical, and public health questions into statistical work: designing studies together with physicians or life scientists, computing sample sizes, writing analysis plans, cleaning and checking data, writing analysis code in SAS or R and similar tools, reporting effect sizes and uncertainty, and explaining results and limitations to research teams, data monitoring committees, or regulatory agencies.
entries.question: What do biostatisticians do every day?

entries.answer: Risks to note in advance include inappropriate design or sample size, post hoc changes to the analysis plan, poor data quality and missing data handling, leakage of participant information, unclear responsibility boundaries in submission materials, and missing review in multi-party collaboration; control depends on a predefined analysis plan, clear permissions, and traceable records.
entries.question: What risks should I pay the most attention to in advance for this job?

entries.answer: Fit signals are being able to turn a research question into a testable analysis plan, being willing to check data and assumptions item by item, accepting that conclusions may be reviewed and revised, and stating the boundaries of a conclusion clearly when data are insufficient; an interest in mathematics or programming alone is not enough to prove competence.
entries.question: How do I judge whether I am suited to being a biostatistician?

entries.answer: AI and statistical software can assist rollback-capable steps such as literature search, code drafts, data dictionary organization, document structure, and chart drafts; study design, sample size determination, missing data handling decisions, effect interpretation, and responsibility for signing results remain with people.
entries.question: Which tasks will AI change?

entries.answer: The definition of endpoints and the analysis population, the missing data handling method, the reasonableness of model assumptions, the statement of conclusions and limitations, and the signing of external submission materials must all be reviewed and owned by trained and authorized people.
entries.question: Which steps must retain human review?

entries.answer: Education and course training, proof of statistical programming ability, institutional authorization, data access and confidentiality agreements, the scope of ethics approval, and the rules for signing statistical reports must each be verified; O*NET lists it as Job Zone Five, and BLS lists a master's degree as the typical entry-level education.
